welcome.title: Welcome — start here
welcome.transcript:
Welcome to White Tee Research, our shared library for building a plain white T-shirt brand.

We are starting with the competitive landscape. Our first three profiles cover ASKET, Son of a Tailor, and True Classic. Each explores the product, price, brand message, customer evidence, and what we might learn. Their current ranges extend beyond a single product, and these first profiles are a starting point, not a complete market survey.

You can listen to audio briefs directly on this site. Use the play and pause controls, drag the progress bar to skip ahead, or download the MP3. The transcript stays tucked away until you select Show transcript. Audio is generated locally on our Mac from written text, without a paid speech service.

Later, the research will inform our customer persona, brand direction, and website plan. Archetype branding, persuasion principles, and modern or postmodern design are possibilities to explore, not decisions we have already made.

To improve any page, use Suggest a change. It opens a GitHub issue with the page link included. A GitHub account is required, and submitted feedback is public.

asket.title: Listen to the 60-second ASKET brief
asket.transcript:
ASKET shows how a plain white T-shirt can compete on detail.

In our November ninth research, its white tee cost sixty-five dollars. It uses organic long-staple cotton, with three length options and production in Portugal. ASKET now sells a broader essentials collection, so it is a product benchmark for us, rather than a single-product business.

Its likely appeal is to shoppers who want understated clothing and specific information about fit and materials. We interpret its brand personality as the Sage, with Creator cues: explain the product, then keep refining it.

Through Cialdini's lens, production knowledge offers authority cues, while customer reviews provide social proof. These are interpretations of its messaging, not proof that it increases sales.

Our takeaway: make quality visible through fabric details, fit guidance, and clear photographs. Before adopting premium pricing ourselves, test the shirt's opacity, wash performance, and whether customers value different lengths.

son-of-a-tailor.title: Listen to the 60-second Son of a Tailor brief
son-of-a-tailor.transcript:
Son of a Tailor makes fit the reason to choose its T-shirt.

In our November ninth research, the cotton tee cost seventy-five dollars. It offered Supima cotton, custom or standard sizing, and made-to-order production in Portugal. Production takes seven to ten days before delivery, and the white fabric is described as slightly translucent.

Its likely audience values personal fit enough to consider a higher price and a wait. We read its personality as the Creator, supported by Sage cues: individual craftsmanship explained through a sizing process.

Through Cialdini's lens, production expertise suggests authority, while displayed reviews offer social proof. The first-order remake primarily reduces risk; it is not automatically reciprocity or a refund promise.

For our white tee, the lesson is to explain fit and material tradeoffs clearly. Test whether customers need custom manufacturing, or whether a useful size guide and straightforward fit choices solve their problem.

true-classic.title: Listen to the 60-second True Classic brief
true-classic.transcript:
True Classic sells the promise of looking good in an everyday T-shirt.

In our November ninth research, its white crew neck showed a regular price of thirty-four ninety-nine, with a lower promotional price. The fabric was a cotton and polyester blend, with several length and hem choices. The brand now sells a wider clothing range.

Its likely appeal is to shoppers seeking flattering fit, comfort, and value. We interpret its personality as the Everyperson: relatable clothing for everyday situations, with an added promise of confidence.

Customer counts, reviews, and try-on videos make social proof prominent. Relatable presentation may also support liking. A sale label alone does not prove genuine scarcity, and the review totals have not been independently audited by us.

For our brand, test clear try-on photographs with useful sizing context. Compare a simple single-shirt offer with bundles, and investigate durability and guarantee terms before copying the sales approach.

jil-sander.title: Listen to the 60-second Jil Sander brief
jil-sander.transcript:
Jil Sander is a reference for making a simple product feel carefully considered.

The German designer established her company and first collection in nineteen sixty-eight. Her work combines minimalism with technical and material experimentation. We are studying her approach as a designer, rather than treating every later collection from her namesake label as her own work.

For our plain white T-shirt, the useful lesson is precision. Pay attention to the neckline, fabric weight, stitching, and proportions. A restrained design still needs details that justify a closer look.

On the website, use clear product photographs, readable type, and specific facts about the shirt. Help shoppers understand quality instead of relying on the word premium.

Try sketching one product page with a full-shirt photograph, a fabric close-up, and three concrete facts. Ask a classmate what explains the price. These are our applications of Sander's work, not recommendations or an endorsement from her.

christophe-lemaire.title: Listen to the 60-second Christophe Lemaire brief
christophe-lemaire.transcript:
Christophe Lemaire offers a useful reference for clothing designed around everyday life.

The French designer founded his label in nineteen ninety-one, after working in Paris fashion studios. He later led artistic direction at Lacoste and Hermès. At Lemaire, creative work is shared with Sarah-Linh Tran, with attention to movement, materials, and layering.

For our white T-shirt, focus on how the garment behaves during a normal day. Test its length and drape while sitting, reaching, and wearing another layer. A standing product photograph cannot answer every question about comfort or fit.

On the website, show the same tee alone and under an overshirt. Explain useful fit details in everyday language so customers can judge how it might work for them.

Try photographing a sample in three ordinary situations. Ask classmates which images help them choose a size. These are our proposed lessons from the designers' work, not their recommendations for our brand.

rei-kawakubo.title: Listen to the 60-second Rei Kawakubo brief
rei-kawakubo.transcript:
Rei Kawakubo is a reference for questioning what clothing can be.

The Japanese designer founded Comme des Garçons. Her work explores boundaries between clothing, the body, and art. The Metropolitan Museum of Art devoted its twenty-seventeen exhibition to that approach.

For our plain white T-shirt, the lesson is to question an assumption before adding decoration. Must the shirt be fitted? Must it be symmetrical? Must it be presented as an undershirt? These questions can help us find a distinct point of view while we decide what customers actually need.

On the website, experiment with image crops or editorial layouts, but keep price, sizing, and buying controls easy to find. An unusual presentation should still be understandable.

Try making two mood boards for the same tee: one quiet and one experimental. Ask classmates what each suggests about the wearer and price. These are our applications of Kawakubo's work, not recommendations from her.
